extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, students of literature, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing and judging poetic works—especially tragedy—including definitions of elements (plot, character, thought, diction, spectacle), rules for unity, plot construction (reversal, recognition, denouement), and poetic diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as the principle of the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and allied arts are modes of imitation (mimesis) — a common principle underlying poetry, music, dance, painting, and sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish artistic forms by asking how they imitate: consider the medium, the objects imitated, and the manner of imitation. This conceptual foundation determines how one judges or composes works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium (the 'maternal vehicle') of imitation in the arts is rhythm, language, and 'harmony' (melody), taken singly or in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and balance medium(s) appropriately for the genre (e.g., tragedy uses language and melody); the chosen medium shapes possible effects and techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation (high vs low types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arts differ by the objects they represent: higher or lower types may be imitated; in poetry this distinction underpins the separation of tragedy and comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the subject is a higher (noble) or lower (base) type—this will determine tone, moral purpose, and suitable modes of representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation (dramatic vs narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may be dramatic (drama), narrative (epic or lyrical narrative), or a mixture; manner of imitation affects form and audience engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose dramatic presentation when action is to be enacted and shown; choose narrative when length and breadth of action are required. Be aware of differences in unity and modes of presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy and its six elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is defined by six elements: three external—Spectacle (opsis), Song/lyric (melos), Diction (lexis); and three internal—Plot (mythos), Character (ethos), and Thought (dianoia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot is primary; character and thought are secondary. When evaluating or composing tragedy, analyze how each of the six elements contributes to the whole and to the elicitation of pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot (the representation of the action) is of primary importance in tragedy; character and thought follow in importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the plot is well-constructed and drives the emotional effects; character and thought should serve the requirements of the plot rather than replace it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must be a Whole (completeness and magnitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must be a whole — complete in itself — and of adequate magnitude for its purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good plot has a beginning, middle, and end such that each part follows inevitably or probably from what precedes; it must neither be fragmentary nor excessively long for its unified action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (not unity of hero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot consists in unity of action (a single coherent causal or probable sequence), not merely in the unity of the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid multiple disconnected actions; all incidents must contribute organically to the single action; incidents must follow by probability or necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic connection of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The parts of a plot must be organically connected—each incident linked to others so that the whole is cohesive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing, ensure episodes, choral odes, prologues, and scenes integrate with the central action rather than feel appended or episodic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic (universal) truth over historical (particular) truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry expresses the universal (what generally happens or what is characteristically true), whereas history records the particular; poetic truth permits idealization necessary for unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When artistic truth conflicts with factual detail, privilege the universal and probable necessities of dramatic truth to secure unity and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of probable or necessary sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents must follow one another by probable or necessary sequence (causal or logically convincing transitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use probability/necessity to justify links between events; avoid arbitrary or disconnected incidents that violate expectations without poetic reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of the Inevitable and the Unexpected
rubrics_metrics.description: The best tragic effects arise from combining inevitability (necessity) and unexpectedness (surprise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct reversals and recognitions so that outcomes feel necessary in retrospect yet are surprising in the moment—this produces pity and fear effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple and Complex Plots; Reversal and Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots may be simple (change of fortune without recognition) or complex (including reversal [peripeteia] and recognition [anagnorisis]); reversal and recognition are defined devices producing tragic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversal and recognition deliberately: define their kinds, set them up with causal plausibility, and integrate them into the unified action to maximize catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative Parts of Tragedy (prologue, episodes, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is composed of quantitative parts—prologue, episodes, choral odes, etc.—each having a function in the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange these parts to serve the plot's unity and emotional arc; beware interpolations that disrupt organic order (the text notes some interpolations historically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of fortune and character suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic action requires a change of fortune appropriate to the character; the character's nature must make the change credible and moving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a hero whose moral configuration and choices make the catastrophe intelligible. An unhappy ending is more truly tragic than contrived poetic justice favored by popular taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity and fear must arise from the plot itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The emotions of pity and fear should spring from the plot's internal necessities, not from spectacle or scenic trickery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on scenery, stagecraft, or sensational effects to produce catharsis; cultivate incidents and character choices that generate emotions intrinsically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as manifestation of moral purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Character shows moral purpose (ethos); ethical portraiture requires plausibility—necessity and probability apply to character formation as to plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict consistent, believable motives; idealize character where necessary but maintain an inner necessity so that actions remain credible and meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Deus Ex Machina
rubrics_metrics.description: Arbitrary contrivances (deus ex machina) that resolve the plot from outside the organic action are condemned or treated as out of place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist last-minute external solutions that negate the plot's internal logic; solutions should arise from the established action and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical craft rules for the tragic poet
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical guidance: (1) place the scene vividly before the poet's eyes and act the parts to enter into sympathy with characters; (2) sketch the bare outline of the action before filling in episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use embodiment and rehearsal to understand characters; plan the plot structure top-down (outline first) so episodes fill into a coherent unified action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful management of complication and denouement
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful about the complication (peripeteia/plot complication) and the denouement—especially the denouement's ordering and plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure complications arise naturally and the dénouement follows as the necessary consequence; avoid rushed or implausible resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unify varied forms of poetic excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: If possible, combine varied forms of poetic excellence (plot, character, diction, song, spectacle) into an organic whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for works where lyric, dialogue, and dramatic action enhance rather than compete; avoid mismatches (e.g., epic details in a tightly unified tragedy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overcharge tragedy with epic details
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overburdening a tragedy with details and elements appropriate to epic poetry (lengthy narrative digressions, excessive episodes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the concentrated tragic effect by resisting epic expansiveness unless it serves unity and magnitude; maintain focus on the single action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choral odes must be organic
rubrics_metrics.description: Choral odes (chorus songs) should form an organic part of the whole and not be irrelevant interruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate choral material so it comments on, deepens, or advances the plot and emotion; avoid independent lyrical excursions that fracture unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) and Diction (lexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (the intellectual element) is expressed in speeches composed according to rhetorical rules; diction relates closely to delivery and the art of speaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose speeches that reveal thought through rhetorically appropriate structures; select diction mindful of performance and the poet's aim for clarity, propriety, and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction and the admissible use of metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic diction prescribes the words and modes of speech admissible in poetry, including metaphor; language should balance elevation and perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphor judiciously to elevate without sacrificing clarity; adapt diction to the genre and to the audience's comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevation combined with perspicuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should combine elevated language with perspicuity (clear intelligibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obscurity for its own sake; elevated expression must still convey universal truths intelligibly to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs. Tragedy: length, metre, and plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic and tragedy share unity of action but differ in length, metre, and techniques for making incredible fiction plausible; tragedy attains concentrated effect within narrower limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing epic or tragic mode, account for audience, desired unity, and the concentration of effect; use metre and plausibility techniques appropriate to the chosen mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling critical objections (poetic truth vs. reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond to objections by distinguishing poetic truth from ordinary reality: justify apparent impossibilities by artistic requirements or received opinion; a probable impossibility is preferable to an improbable possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defend artistic departures from fact by appeal to higher aims of art or typical/accepted beliefs; ensure deviations serve the poem's universal truth and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for resolving textual or interpretive difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation methods include resolving via metaphor, accent/breathing, punctuation, ambiguity of meaning, and usage—choose the reading that best fits poetic sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When faced with textual or semantic puzzles, prefer interpretations that restore coherence, metrical sense, and alignment with the poem's universal meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrational or morally hurtful elements without necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational elements or depravity of character are censured when introduced without inner necessity; they must have an operative dramatic reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce morally problematic aspects only if they arise naturally from character or plot necessity and contribute to the universal truth or emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five sources of censure and the need to answer them
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism arises from five sources: that something is impossible, irrational, morally hurtful, contradictory, or contrary to artistic correctness; answers should be sought under the accepted critical heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or defending a work, anticipate these criticisms and ensure the work provides internal justifications (probability, necessity, artistic rationale) under the corresponding categories.
